t.6.5.1: That army, well guarded and thoroughly composed, was duly and properly encamped by Nīla on the northern shore of the ocean.
t.6.5.2: And Mainda and Dvivida, both of them bulls among the monkeys, moved about there on every side of that army in order to guard it.
t.6.5.3: When the army had encamped on the shore of the lord of rivers and streams, Rāma, seeing Lakṣmaṇa standing at his side, spoke these words.
t.6.5.4: Grief, they say, surely passes away with the passing of time; but for me, who do not see my beloved, it grows day by day.
t.6.5.5: It is no grief to me that my beloved is far away, nor is it grief to me that she has been carried off; this alone do I lament, that her youth is passing away.
t.6.5.6: Blow, O wind, to where the maiden is; having touched her, touch me as well. Through you my body touches hers, and in the moon our eyes meet.
t.6.5.7: That which my beloved cried out to me as she was being carried away, “Ah, my lord!”, burns my limbs like poison drunk and lying in the stomach.
t.6.5.8: Night and day my body is burned by the fire of love, whose fuel is separation from her and whose blazing flames are my thoughts of her.
t.6.5.9: Plunging into the ocean, O Saumitri, I shall sleep there without you; then this blazing passion could scarcely burn me as I lie asleep in the water.
t.6.5.10: This is much for one who is filled with longing; by this alone it is possible to live, that I and she of lovely thighs abide upon one and the same earth.
t.6.5.11: Like a dry field that draws moisture from a well-watered field beside it, I live on that seeping moisture, in that I hear she is alive.
t.6.5.12: When indeed, having conquered my enemies, shall I behold Sītā, with her lovely hips and eyes long like lotus petals, like Śrī herself in her abundant splendor?
t.6.5.13: When, oh when, shall I gently raise her lotus-like face, with its lovely lips red as the bimba fruit, and drink from it as a sick man drinks a life-giving elixir?
t.6.5.14: When indeed will those full breasts of hers, pressed close together and like palm fruits, come to me, trembling, as she laughs?
t.6.5.15: Surely she, the dark-eyed one, finding herself amid the rākṣasas, though I am her protector, finds no rescuer, as if she had no protector at all.
t.6.5.16: When will she, having shaken the Rākṣasas and cast them off, rise up and escape, like the crescent of the moon in autumn, having cast off the dark clouds?
t.6.5.17: Sītā, slender by nature, has surely become slenderer still through grief and fasting, owing to her adverse circumstances of place and time.
t.6.5.18: When indeed, having lodged my arrows in the chest of the lord of the Rākṣasas, shall I bring Sītā back and cast off the sorrow of my heart?
t.6.5.19: When indeed will the virtuous Sītā, who is like a daughter of the immortals, clasp me by the neck in her longing and shed tears born of joy?
t.6.5.20: When shall I suddenly cast off this terrible grief, born of my separation from Maithilī, as one casts off a soiled garment?
t.6.5.21: While the wise Rāma was thus lamenting there, the sun, its orb grown dim with the waning of the day, went down to its setting.
t.6.5.22: Consoled by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma performed the twilight worship, remembering lotus-petal-eyed Sītā, overwhelmed with grief.
